source_text: CAPUT DECIMUMSEPTIMUM, De potentia Dei exsequente. Atque haec quoque de voluntate Dei: Sequitur agendi potentia, quae est vita Dei, qua pro libertate voluntatis suae extrinsecus operari potest, quaecunque libere velle potest, operatur, quaecunque libere vult. Potentiam Deo recte tribui, sacrae literae satis declarant, Gen. XVII.1; XXVIII.3; XXXV.11; Jerem. XXXII.18-19; Psal. XCI; Luc. I.37; Apoc. IV.8; XI.17; XIX.6.
english: CHAPTER SEVENTEEN. On Gods executive power.

And these things also concerning the will of God: there follows the power of acting, which is Gods life by which, according to the liberty of His will, He can work outwardly — whatever He can freely will, He works, whatever He freely wills.
That power is rightly attributed to God, the sacred writings sufficiently declare — Genesis 17:1; 28:3; 35:11; Jeremiah 32:18-19; Psalm 91; Luke 1:37; Revelation 4:8; 11:17; 19:6.

source_text: Verum potentiae nomine hic non intelligimus passivam potentiam, quippe quae in Deum, purum actum, cadere nequit, neque actum quo Deus intus in seipso e naturae suae necessaria perfectione semper agit, ac proinde neque potentiam generandi et spirandi, quippe qua naturaliter agit et ad intra: sed potentiam activam seu exsequentem, qua extrinsecus operari potest, et, quandocunque lubet, operatur. Sub qua operatione etiam impeditionem, permissionem, ordinationem comprehensam volumus, quam, dirigente intellectu, voluntas imperat. Neque hanc Deo tribuimus ea notione qua Aristoteles V. Metaph. finit, principium transmutationis in aliud secundum quod aliud: nam talis potentia activa competit enti creato et finito, in quo actus et potentia differunt. Deo autem potentia activa tribuitur secundum perfectionem, non secundum participationem, et in eo potentia et actus sunt idem. Hinc Richardus de Sancto Victore: Constans est Deum esse potentem potentiae plenitudine, non potentiae participatione.
english: But by the name of power here we do not understand passive power, which cannot fall upon God as pure act, nor the act by which God inwardly in Himself always acts from the necessary perfection of His nature, and therefore neither the power of generating and spirating, by which He acts naturally and inwardly: but active or executive power, by which He can work outwardly and, whenever it pleases Him, does work.

Under this operation we also will to comprise impeding, permitting, and ordering, which, with the intellect directing, the will commands. Nor do we attribute this to God in the notion by which Aristotle in Metaphysics V defines a principle of change into another according as it is other: for such active power belongs to created and finite being, in which act and power differ. But to God active power is attributed according to perfection, not according to participation, and in Him power and act are the same. Hence Richard of Saint Victor: It is certain that God is powerful by fullness of power, not by participation of power.

source_text: II. Est autem in ea considerandum objectum, conditio et distinctio. III. Objectum est omne id, quod Deus ut ens verum ac possibile infinito intellectu suo comprehensum, libere velle potest. Nam quicquid Deus libere velle potest, id ipsum etiam facere potest; et quicquid facere potest, id ipsum libere velle potest. Potest autem Deus ea duntaxat libere velle, quae essentiae ipsius et naturali voluntati non sunt contraria et ab intellectu ipsius infinito tanquam entia vera, saltem possibilia, comprehendi possunt. Possibilitas rei principiative ab intellectu Dei, formaliter vero ex ratione rerum formali. Unde non propter potentiam Dei, sed propter formalem repugnantiam rei, nulla est potentia respectu contradictoriorum. Et hinc Deus dicitur facere posse omnia possibilia, quae congruunt ipsius naturae, intellectui et voluntati: caetera omnia impossibilia, quippe quae contradictionem, impotentiam, perversitatem, mendacium continent — ut Deum alium facere, mutari, mentiri, peccare, efficere ut aliquid simul sit et non sit. Cum autem haec a Deo fieri posse negamus, non facimus potentiae illius infinitae injuriam, sed cavemus ne essentiae, intellectui et voluntati Dei incongrua tribuantur. Confer Luc. I.37; XVIII.27; Marc. XIV.36; Jac. I.17; Psal. V.5; Num. XXIII.19; II Tim. II.13.
english: II. But in it there is to be considered the object, the condition, and the distinction. III. The object is everything which God, as true and possible being comprehended by His infinite intellect, can freely will. For whatever God can freely will, that same He can also do; and whatever He can do, that same He can freely will.

But God can freely will only those things which are not contrary to His essence and natural will and which can be comprehended by His infinite intellect as true beings, at least as possible. Possibility of a thing is principally from Gods intellect, but formally from the formal reason of things. Hence not because of Gods power, but because of formal repugnance of the thing, there is no power with respect to contradictories.

And hence God is said to be able to do all possibles which agree with His nature, intellect, and will: all the rest are impossible, inasmuch as they contain contradiction, impotence, perversity, falsehood — as to make another God, to be changed, to lie, to sin, to make something simultaneously be and not be. When we deny that these can be done by God, we do not injure His infinite power, but we take care that things incongruous to Gods essence, intellect, and will not be attributed. Compare Luke 1:37; 18:27; Mark 14:36; James 1:17; Psalm 5:5; Numbers 23:19; 2 Timothy 2:13.

source_text: IV. Conditio ejus est triplex: universalitas, immensitas, perfectio in opere. V. Universalitas est, qua Deus omnia potest quae velle potest. VI. Immensitas est, qua Deus potentia sua omnia penetrat et ambit. VII. Perfectio in opere est, qua Deus optime facit quicquid facit. Hinc Moses Gen. I.31: Tum inspexisse Deum omnia quae fecerat, et ecce bona valde. Ad extremum huic potentiae Dei non subjicitur factum sub ratione facti, sed sub ratione fiendi. Et ideo eadem potentia qua potuit creare mundum, non factum, sed faciendum, quod in potentia facientis est et non in actu factus.
english: IV. Its condition is threefold: universality, immensity, perfection in the work. V. Universality is that by which God can do all things which He can will. VI. Immensity is that by which God by His power penetrates and encompasses all things. VII. Perfection in the work is that by which God does most excellently whatever He does. Hence Moses in Genesis 1:31: Then God looked upon all things which He had made, and behold, they were very good.

Finally, to this power of God what is already done is not subject under the reason of the done, but under the reason of being done. And therefore by the same power by which He could create the world, it is not as already made, but as to-be-made, which is in the power of the maker and not already made in act.

source_text: VIII. Distinctio est, qua potentia Dei est absoluta aut ordinata. Absoluta dicitur quia non est limitata universali lege naturae, quasi praeter et supra illam Deus non possit aliquid agere; et sic dicitur in comparatione ad ordinatam, qua praecise agit juxta communem legem et ordinem decretorum suorum. IX. Absoluta potentia est, qua Deus agere potest quicquid vult et velle potest, praeter ordinem naturae per providentiam a se positum, legesque universales, judiciumque particulare inde deductum. Dicitur etiam extraordinaria, qua miracula Deus edit praeter, supra, et, si cum Graecis loquaris, contra naturae leges universales et communes a se positas. Natura dicitur tripliciter secundum Augustinum: 1. solitus naturae cursus; 2. vis activa et passiva; 3. natura naturans, scilicet Deus. Quapropter quaedam sunt supra naturam, quaedam contra naturam, quaedam praeter naturam. Deus igitur facit contra naturam primo modo dictam in omnibus miraculis; sed contra naturam secundo et tertio modo dictam nunquam aliquid facit. Sic ergo Deus nihil facit contra naturam, sed supra et praeter eam. X. Ordinata est, a qua Deus secundum ordinem per providentiam suam constitutum praecise, legibus universalibus et particularibus judiciis inde deductis conformiter operatur. Dicitur quoque ordinaria; hac Deus omnia a se creata etiamnum aut conservat aut moderatur aut destruit; hac communiter efficit omnia in omnibus, pro beneplacito voluntatis suae.
english: VIII. The distinction is that by which Gods power is absolute or ordained. Absolute is so called because it is not limited by the universal law of nature, as if beside and above that God could not do something; and so it is said in comparison with the ordained, by which He acts precisely according to the common law and order of His decrees.

IX. Absolute power is that by which God can do whatever He wills and can will, beside the order of nature placed by Himself through providence, and the universal laws, and the particular judgment drawn from them. It is also called extraordinary, by which God works miracles beside, above, and, if you speak with the Greeks, against the universal and common laws of nature placed by Himself. Nature is said in three ways according to Augustine: 1. the accustomed course of nature; 2. active and passive force; 3. nature naturing, namely God. Therefore some things are above nature, some against nature, some beside nature. God therefore does against nature in the first sense in all miracles; but against nature in the second and third senses He never does anything. Thus God does nothing against nature, but above and beside it.

X. Ordained is that by which God works precisely according to the order constituted by His providence, conformably to universal laws and particular judgments drawn from them. It is also called ordinary; by this God still either conserves or governs or destroys all things created by Himself; by this He commonly works all things in all, according to the good pleasure of His will.

source_text: XI. Sunt autem de omnipotentia Dei quaedam utiles observationes. 1. Soli Deo convenit omnipotentia, quae nulli creaturae, qua tali, communicari potest. Nam potentiae qua creatur mundus et ea quae in mundo sunt, sine coactione, sine impedimento, sine subjecta materia, sine instrumento, sine exemplari externo, creatura non est capax. Omnis enim creatura operatur in subjecta materia; et omnis essentia creata finita est et limitata propriis terminis, ac proinde impossibile est eam referri ad omnia. 2. Potentia Dei, secundum seipsam considerata, abstrahit ab omni tempore, et non determinatur ad tempus, nisi temporali actu vel effectu qui subjectus est omnipotentiae. Sicut fides in articulis credibilibus abstrahit a tempore: tamen secundum quod comparatur ad credentes secundum diversitatem temporum diversimode significatur. Unde antiqui patres crediderunt Christum incarnandum, passurum et resurrecturum; nos credimus Christum incarnatum, passum, mortuum, resurrexisse. Dicit autem Augustinus: Tempora variata sunt, fides immutata permansit. Ita et de potentia: eadem potentia est quae ad unum est et ad idem secundum omnem differentiam temporum; sed ad diversa tempora determinatur cum dicitur potuit creare mundum, et potuit creatus esse a se mundus.
english: XI. But there are certain useful observations concerning Gods omnipotence. 1. Omnipotence belongs to God alone, and cannot be communicated to any creature as such. For of the power by which the world and the things in the world are created without compulsion, without hindrance, without subject matter, without instrument, without external exemplar, the creature is not capable. For every creature works in subject matter; and every created essence is finite and limited by its own bounds, and therefore it is impossible that it be referred to all things.

2. Gods power, considered according to itself, abstracts from all time, and is not determined to time except by a temporal act or effect which is subject to omnipotence. Just as faith in believable articles abstracts from time: yet according as it is compared to believers according to diversity of times it is signified diversely. Hence the ancient fathers believed Christ was to be incarnate, to suffer, and to rise; we believe Christ has been incarnate, has suffered, has died, has risen. But Augustine says: Times have varied, faith has remained unchanged. So also concerning power: it is the same power which is toward one and the same according to every difference of times; but it is determined to diverse times when it is said He could create the world, and the world could have been created by Him.

source_text: 3. Quia res in seipsa variatur secundum differentiam temporis, ideo, cum loquimur de potentia secundum quod refertur ad rem, necesse est ut diversis loquendi formis utamur. Sic Deus aliquando fuit ex potentia facturus, et aliquando ex eadem potentia facit, et aliquando fecit. Facturum esse non est facere, et facere non est fecisse. Et ideo non sequitur: quicquid Deus potuit facere, potest semper facere, quia ante rem potuit aliquid facere cum res non esset nisi in potentia, quod non potest facere cum res perfecta est. Sed recte sequitur: quicquid aliquando potuit facere, semper potest facere, dummodo potentia facientis semper sit ad illud. 4. Verum quidem est quod quicquid est in Deo, actus est et nihil in potentia: tamen non sequitur ex hoc quod quicquid potuit facere, semper possit facere. Potentia enim est respectu ejus quod fieri potest, et non respectu ejus quod factum est. Quapropter haec propositio: quicquid Deus aliquando potuit facere, semper potest facere, simpliciter neganda est. Haec autem est vera: quicquid Deus aliquando potuit facere et est de subjecto divinae potentiae, hoc semper potest facere. 5. Ex omnipotentia Dei non potest concludi aliquid esse aut fore, nisi constet de voluntate Dei. Ratio haec est, quia voluntas Dei libera potentiam ad hoc illudve agendum determinat, et Deus propterea aliquid facit quia id facere vult — Dan. III.17-18; Rom. IV.20-21; Matth. VIII.2; Luc. I. Idcirco hic locum habet illud, rationem captivandam esse sub obsequium fidei, quando nempe de voluntate Dei constat, etiamsi mens nostra possibilitatem rei non capiat. Confer Calv. Inst. IV.16.24. CAPUT DECIMUM OCTAVUM, De attributis Dei tertii generis, sequitur.
english: 3. Because a thing in itself varies according to difference of time, therefore when we speak of power as referred to the thing, it is necessary that we use diverse forms of speaking. Thus God at one time was about to make from power, and at another time from the same power He makes, and at another He has made. To be about to make is not to make, and to make is not to have made. And therefore it does not follow: whatever God could do, He can always do, because before the thing He could do something when the thing was only in potency, which He cannot do when the thing is perfected. But it rightly follows: whatever He could at some time do, He can always do, provided the makers power is always toward that.

4. It is indeed true that whatever is in God is act and nothing in potency: yet it does not follow from this that whatever He could do He can always do. For power is with respect to that which can be done, and not with respect to that which has been done. Therefore this proposition — whatever God could at some time do, He can always do — is simply to be denied. But this is true: whatever God could at some time do and is of the subject of divine power, this He can always do.

5. From Gods omnipotence it cannot be concluded that something is or will be, unless it is established concerning Gods will. The reason is this: because Gods free will determines power to doing this or that, and God therefore does something because He wills to do it — Daniel 3:17-18; Romans 4:20-21; Matthew 8:2; Luke 1. Therefore here that saying has place, that reason is to be taken captive under the obedience of faith, namely when Gods will is established, even if our mind does not grasp the possibility of the thing. Compare Calvin, Institutes 4.16.24. CHAPTER EIGHTEEN, On Gods attributes of the third genus, follows.
